I am fifty-five years old and I have been farming these eight *mu* of land in Quzhou for more than thirty years. Around here, everyone knows the only sensible way to make a living from the soil is the winter wheat–summer maize rotation. The wheat goes in right after the National Day holiday in early October, sleeps through the winter under the snow, and comes off the combine in early June. The very same day we thresh the wheat, we plant the summer maize. By late September the maize is dry enough to harvest, and then we plough and ready the ground for wheat again. I would never gamble on cotton or vegetables—the market is too uncertain and the labour too much for a man my age.

This year I will stick to what I know. I have 8 *mu* of good flat land. For the wheat I will buy an improved variety such as *Jimai 22* or *Liangxing 99* from the seed dealer in town—about 30 *jin* of seed per *mu*. For the maize I will plant a hybrid like *Denghai 605*, one and a half packages per *mu*, because the hybrids yield better and stand up to the wind. 

I will rotary-till the wheat field before sowing to break up the corn stubble and level the ground. For the maize I see no need to till again after the wheat harvest; I will just plant directly into the stubble to save time and fuel, the way my neighbours do.

Fertiliser is expensive, but I have learned that if you skimp on it the crop punishes you. For the wheat I will spread one 50 *kg* bag of compound fertiliser (about 15–15–15) as a basal dose at sowing, and then top-dress with another 50 *kg* of urea at green-up or jointing. For the maize I will put down roughly 80 *kg* of compound fertiliser at planting and leave it at that. 

Irrigation depends on the sky, but in a normal year I water the wheat three times—once before winter to help it establish, once at jointing, and once at filling. The maize usually needs two good flood irrigations, one at the jointing stage and another at the big flare stage, drawn from our village well.

Pests and weeds are a constant worry. I will spray the wheat four times: herbicide once after sowing, insecticide twice when aphids and armyworms show up, and fungicide once at heading to keep the rust away. The maize gets three sprays—herbicide at the three-leaf stage, insecticide twice for corn borers and aphids, and I will add a fungicide if the weather turns wet.

If the season treats me fairly, I expect about 1,000 *jin* (500 *kg*) of wheat per *mu* and about 1,100 *jin* (550 *kg*) of maize per *mu*. That is enough to feed my family, sell the surplus, and cover the costs of next year’s inputs.
